title: Nothing to envy
hook: keep death and exile before your eyes daily, and you won't grasp or envy (Enchiridion 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the insult. Your line was a breath before. Did you put one breath between a sting and your reply? Day three hundred fifty-three.

Two words sit at the start of section twenty-one, and neither one is cheerful: death and exile. It's a strange place to look for a cure for envy. Envy looks sideways, at a neighbor's new kitchen, a friend's easy promotion, the couple whose photos never seem to have a bad day. Epictetus points somewhere else entirely, and he asks for it every day, not once in a while. The note in the handbook is short and blunt. And the payoff he promises is an odd one. Today: nothing to envy.
screen: `DEATH AND EXILE.` → `ENVY LOOKS SIDEWAYS.` → `EVERY DAY, NOT ONCE IN A WHILE.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. Let death and exile, and everything that seems terrible, be before your eyes every day, Epictetus says, and death most of all. Second, the promise. Then, he says, you'll never think anything low or petty, and you'll never want anything too much. Notice what he doesn't promise. Not that you'll be less afraid, or more cheerful. He promises a change in what you want. Third, how it works. Envy depends on a sense that the thing you envy is huge. Their promotion, their renovation, their perfect vacation. Set it in the light of death and it shrinks to its real size, not worthless, just the size of something that will be left behind. The Stoics weren't alone here. In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates calls philosophy a kind of practice for dying. The Latin phrase memento mori, remember you'll die, names the same habit. Fourth, the gentle part. This isn't meant to darken the day. Done gently, it can work the other way. The coffee tastes like coffee. The annoying coworker becomes a person who will also die, which is strangely tender. And envy, that tight, sour feeling, loosens, because in this light there's nothing to win. Everyone at the table, the one with the new car and the one with the old bike, is on the same short visit. Epictetus says it plainly: keep it before your eyes, and you won't grasp. If death feels too heavy today, start with exile: picture leaving behind everything you own. It does the same quiet work.
screen: `DEATH AND EXILE, BEFORE YOUR EYES.` · `NOTHING PETTY, NOTHING TOO MUCH.` · `ENVY SHRINKS TO ITS REAL SIZE.` · `THE SAME SHORT VISIT.` · then, large: `NOTHING TO ENVY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you envy. Someone's house, job, body, ease. See it clearly. Now gently widen the picture. Fifty years from now, or a hundred. The house belongs to strangers. The job is a line in a story nobody tells. The person is gone, and so are you. Hold it without fear, the way you'd look at the sea. Then look back at the thing you envied, and see what size it is now. The bell holds the time.
Memento mori. Latin for remember you'll die; Epictetus' daily habit: keep death and exile before your eyes, and you'll want nothing too much. Today's word.
Your line: on the same short visit. When envy pinches today, widen the picture for one breath, and let the thing shrink to its real size. Day three hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners briefly bring death or loss to mind each day, as a way of loosening envy and grasping rather than as a source of fear.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): rewrote the hook, which rested on uncited history (Musonius' exile, Domitian's expulsion, emperors killing senators) and said Epictetus 'wrote' the handbook (Arrian recorded it); cut the 'many traditions' and 'people who try it often report' claims; fixed a garbled line; replaced the Musonius/expulsion match pairs and myth with items from the teach.
Enchiridion 21 paraphrased (death, exile and all terrible things daily before your eyes, death most; you will never think anything abject nor desire anything extravagantly). Confirm.
Musonius Rufus exiled by Nero to Gyaros (c. 65 CE): confirm.
Epictetus' departure from Rome under Domitian's expulsion: date uncertain (89 or c. 93–95).
'he had seen emperors kill senators for a sentence in a speech': general claim about the Neronian/Domitianic court; soften if needed.
memento mori as a later Latin phrase: confirm; Phaedo 64a / 67e on philosophy as practice for dying: confirm.
